title: CBI Chargesheet Reveals How NTA Experts Leaked NEET Papers Using Chits and Memory
excerpt: Thirteen people have been charged in the multi-state NEET-UG 2026 paper leak syndicate, with the CBI detailing how testing agency insiders memorized questions and smuggled them out on handwritten notes.
body:
• The CBI has filed a chargesheet charging 13 people in the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak, including NTA insiders who exploited their access to exam content.
  • Testing agency experts memorized questions during the paper-setting process and smuggled them out using handwritten chits, the chargesheet alleges.
  • The investigation describes a multi-state syndicate that exploited systemic shortcomings in NTA's security protocols.
  • The revelations deepen a crisis around India's premier medical entrance exam, which has faced repeated integrity challenges in recent years.

The Central Bureau of Investigation has filed a chargesheet laying out in granular detail how insiders at the National Testing Agency leaked questions from the NEET-UG 2026 medical entrance examination, charging 13 individuals in what it describes as a multi-state paper leak syndicate.

Memorizing and Smuggling Questions

According to the CBI's chargesheet, NTA-appointed subject matter experts exploited their privileged access to exam content during the paper-setting and review process. The experts, who were trusted with handling highly sensitive examination material, allegedly memorized questions during closed-door sessions and later reproduced them on handwritten chits that were smuggled out of secure facilities.

The method was deliberately low-tech, apparently designed to evade the electronic surveillance measures NTA had in place at its paper-setting centers. By relying on human memory and physical notes rather than digital devices, the accused were able to bypass security checks that focused primarily on electronic gadgets and storage media.

"NTA experts turned conspirators — the very people entrusted with safeguarding the exam became the ones who compromised it."

— CBI chargesheet details, as reported by The New Indian Express

Systemic NTA Shortcomings Enabled the Leak

The chargesheet identifies specific shortcomings in NTA's security protocols that created openings for the syndicate. ThePrint reported that the investigation found gaps in how experts were vetted, monitored during paper-setting sessions, and tracked afterward. The absence of rigorous post-session protocols — such as restricting experts' movements or communications immediately after handling exam content — allowed the leaked material to flow quickly to intermediaries.

The syndicate operated across multiple states, with a chain of handlers receiving the leaked questions from the NTA insiders and distributing them to candidates who had paid for advance access. The CBI's investigation traced the network through phone records, financial transactions, and statements from cooperating witnesses.

Deepening Crisis for India's Medical Entrance Exam

The latest revelations add to a growing crisis of confidence around NEET, which serves as the sole gateway for undergraduate medical admissions across India. The exam has faced allegations of irregularities in multiple cycles, with the 2024 edition sparking nationwide protests and a Supreme Court intervention after reports of inflated scores and paper leaks in several states.

The 2026 chargesheet suggests that despite reforms promised after previous scandals, the fundamental vulnerabilities in NTA's exam management infrastructure persist. Education policy experts have called for a complete overhaul of the paper-setting process, including stricter vetting of experts, continuous surveillance during paper-setting sessions, and technology-enabled isolation protocols.

Impact on Students and Diaspora Families

NEET remains a high-stakes exam for millions of Indian families, including thousands in the diaspora whose children prepare to sit for the test to secure medical seats in India. The integrity of the exam directly affects the prospects of students who invest years of preparation, and repeated leak scandals have eroded trust in the system.

The CBI's investigation remains ongoing, with officials indicating that more arrests and chargesheets may follow as the full extent of the syndicate is mapped. The NTA has not issued a detailed public response to the specific allegations in the chargesheet.

The case is expected to be heard in a special CBI court in the coming weeks.
